The 1605 household points to the same holding as the earlier George, within the same parish setting. The surname is specific to this local comparison, and a 19-year interval is straightforward for one adult career. A child bearing George’s name and an adult George participating in his baptism make a continuing local family association more economical than two unconnected Georges. Together these observations warrant probable rather than merely possible cross-record identity. They do not amount to independent proofs of every step.

record_type: printed transcription of Privy Council decree
date: 27 July 1672 decree; Crookshank summary gives 24 July
place: Whitecastle, probably Libberton, Lanarkshire; hearing at Holyroodhouse
source_title: Robert Wodrow, History of the Sufferings of the Church of Scotland (1721), vol.I, appendix no.XLVII, pp.133–134, decree headed 27 July 1672; printed page images freshly inspected
reference: Wodrow vol.I appendix XLVII, pp.133–134; Crookshank vol.I p.285
status: Printed decree and summary page images inspected 17 October 2026; original Council register not inspected
note: The printed decree in Robert Wodrow’s 1721 History, volume I, appendix no. XLVII, pp.133–134, is dated 27 July 1672 in both its heading and Latin opening. It names “James Glasgow in Whitecastle” among people imprisoned for refusing the oath. The monetary fines there belong to Mr James Duncan and the Countess of Wigtoun, not to James Glasgow. William Crookshank’s 1751 summary, volume I p.285, places the same named group under 24 July 1672; preserve that day discrepancy and prefer the printed decree’s 27 July for this source account. Neither source supports the old 1670 date. The two books recount the same proceeding and are not independent evidence of two imprisonments. The surrounding Biggar/Boghall group names men in Biggar, Carwood, Edmonstoun, Worslyd and Carstairs. This favours the Whitecastle in Libberton parish over a location guessed merely from general Covenanter activity. J. L. Davidson’s published article title locates West Whitecastle Farm in Libberton, Lanarkshire (Proceedings of the Society of Antiquaries of Scotland 108, p.383; title checked in the journal’s search-indexed contents, full article not inspected). This supports the Libberton place identification, in the same parish setting as Quothquan and near Biggar’s Lindsaylands; it does not identify a seventeenth-century occupier. This is a probable interpretation of James’s residence, not a parish supplied literally by the decree. White Castle in Garvald and Bara, East Lothian, is a real alternative place. The decree also deals with a Perthshire group; document order alone does not put every accused person in Clydesdale. No kinship is stated.

note: The FamilySearch citation X17D-67M was checked directly: John was born 13 October 1771 and christened 19 October 1771 at Barony, parents Alexander Glasgow and Mary Munro. The copied 3 December 1765 date attached to that same citation is wrong; no independent 1765 record was verified in this review. This corrects the source account, not the vital fields or later identity of either modern John profile. Burke names Agnes Monro, not the documented Mary Munro of Alexander-1309’s couple. Their identity cannot be assumed, and the 1771 child has no inspected occupation, wife or estate bridge identifying him as the merchant rather than the Colinton account John-1304. The merchant’s circa 1770 birth is an inherited estimate, not independent corroboration. Retain both modern Johns and the current father selection, all mothers, vital fields and upstream grades. No new father attachment or merge follows. The 1741 childhood identification of Alexander-1309 is not certified by this review. Exact percentages are subjective judgements, not measured probabilities.

The same narrator calls John his paternal grandfather, born 28 April 1780, and Moses his father. Moses’s Mary J. Pierce marriage on 5 November 1839, Martha W. Thompson marriage in 1848, and 13 January 1892 death match Glasgow-589’s distinctive biography and structured dates. The explicit parent clause and this identity bridge replace the former inference from chronology and marriage/children passages. John Glasgow-209 is documented as the existing father at 94% within this retrospective family-account scope. Subjective 94% for Moses-589 → John-209 as the complete profile pair. This is an undated six-page typescript attributed to William Melanchthon Glasgow, a descendant family account rather than a contemporary birth register or probate. Known date discrepancies elsewhere remain qualifications. Moses’s 1892 death is not John’s death. Exact vital fields, maternity, John’s earlier ancestry and other children’s assessments are unchanged. The already held source was newly inspected for this clause; no new document or father attachment. Maternal review26October2026: page5 first identifies MaryJ.Pierce’s1839 marriage, then says three children were born to Mr.and Mrs.Glasgow—LoisLadd, RobertFinley and JohnCameron. Mary died14March1846; Moses marriedMarthaW.Thompson in1848. Mary is therefore RobertFinley’s named mother in this account; Martha is his later stepmother. This is a retrospective family record, not an inspected original birth/death certificate. It names a different RobertFinley from the1820–1887 namesake. The account places Mary in her twenty-sixth year, meaning age 25; this is compatible with the current birth-before-1821 field and is not a date conflict. This citation and held-e-0cad51964207 refer to the same held document and are not independent corroboration. Lois review, 26 October 2026: the explicit first-marriage child group supports the existing Mary Pierce maternity at subjective 93%, and Martha’s stepmother role without a percentage. Page 5 reports Lois died of consumption in June 1870. This refines the retained 1870 year by a month, not an exact day or place. The account places Mary in her twenty-sixth year, meaning age 25; this is compatible with the current birth-before-1821 field and is not a date conflict. Infant proposal: page 5 names John Cameron Glasgow as an infant child of Moses and Mary J. Pierce and reports death at age 5 months; retain only contextual before-1846 scope, with no exact date/place. Distinct from adult Glasgow-466.

Glasgow-1553.role: The original 1825 will explicitly names Matthew among John’s children and gives him a $200 legacy. Glasgow-36.role: The original will names Taylor as John’s son, gives him a wagon and a joint share of the Antis home tract with James, and appoints James and Taylor executors. Glasgow-664.role: The original will now proves that the Antis/Sinking Valley John had a son John. This independently supports the previously compiled report of a young emigrant son John. The Cambria adult’s reported 1777 Scottish generation, 1820 Allegheny Township household and central Pennsylvania continuity make him the leading checked identity for that son. The will supplies no residence, wife or age for its John, so identification with the Cambria adult remains a probable inference. Daill and Glasgow birthplace claims are not equated or verified.

Glasgow-1984.role: The original will explicitly names a son Samuel and gives him a $50 legacy. Samuel’s reported death before the legacy’s 1832 due date is not a contradiction: the will provides for a deceased child’s issue.

Glasgow-2577.role: The original will names James as a son, joint devisee of the Antis home tract and executor with Taylor. note: Alexander’s independently documented children James, Mary and Ann match the 1892 citation’s Alexander-of-Rasharkin group. That group appears among heirs/next of kin before the separate legatee list. Nancy’s own niece/nephew statements, linked through the Dysart and Anderson baptisms, anchor the family interpretation. John-867’s distinctive James Garvin/Ann branch identifies the other cited household, and his 1846 marriage names father John Glasgow, farmer. Recorded Glasgow birth surnames favor a common paternal family. The combined identity and kinship argument supports a confident 90% inference; a generic unsupported half-sibling possibility does not impose a probable ceiling. The probate citation is an incomplete service notice, not an adjudicated pedigree: Alexander’s living son Robert was omitted. John’s Ballydonnelly description and the cited Lizzie remain unexplained. The underlying petition and heir schedule have not been inspected. These are real limits, but no held competing household matches the James Garvin/Ann group and no evidence identifies different Glasgow fathers through a maternal half-sibling relationship. The flax-grower and older Larne identities remain separate hypotheses.

note: Page 4 names John and Peninnah’s eight children: Hugh, Alexander, Sarah, Moses, Robert, Nancy, Mary and Amy. Alexander was a farmer who moved to Sharon, Iowa and died in 1857. Robert is separately described as unmarried and living at Mount Washington, Pittsburgh. The writer calls John his paternal grandfather and Moses his father. This supplies the parent clause missing from Glasgow-997’s 22 October assessment; the known Iowa Alexander is the compatible profile, supported by the retained Cushing p. 289 Sarah/Alexander-of-Iowa citation. It does not establish Robert as Alexander’s additional given name. The account is retrospective and undated; its Nancy death year (1847) and Peninnah death year (1849) differ from retained profile dates, which are not changed. Nancy’s existing assessment is retained separately. Pages4–5 were also inspected for Moses Thomas Glasgow-589: the fourth child and third son of John, born29October1809 near Bakerstown; his marriages and13January1892 death identify the existing child profile. His father assessment is now94% within retrospective-source scope. held-e-f0fe7f969e32 is an existing citation alias to this same held document, not independent corroboration. Maternal role review: page5 names RobertFinley among Moses and MaryJPierce’s three children, records Mary’s14March1846death, then Moses’s1848 marriage to MarthaWThompson. MaryPierce14470 is Robert2356’s selected mother at93% within this retrospective account; MarthaThompson63146 is his stepmother. The earlier unmarked mother attachment is preserved in import/history and remains unchanged live. No contemporary certificate or gravestone image was inspected. Lois review, 26 October 2026: the explicit first-marriage child group supports the existing Mary Pierce maternity at subjective 93%, and Martha’s stepmother role without a percentage. Page 5 reports Lois died of consumption in June 1870. This refines the retained 1870 year by a month, not an exact day or place. The account places Mary in her twenty-sixth year, meaning age 25; this is compatible with the current birth-before-1821 field and is not a date conflict. Infant proposal: page 5 names John Cameron Glasgow as an infant child of Moses and Mary J. Pierce and reports death at age 5 months; retain only contextual before-1846 scope, with no exact date/place. Distinct from adult Glasgow-466.

note: The visually checked 1903 family memorial, PDF p.17, explicitly names William Glasgow of Killycorragh and Nancy Glendinning as parents of five sons, Henry Cunningham, Adam, Isaac Watts, Benjamin and Alexander Flemming, and three daughters, Mary, Matilda and Jane. Nancy’s reported April 1803 birth and 20 March 1890 Belle Center death anchor this particular family. This is a retrospective family publication, not an original baptism register. Earlier WikiTree Space citations derive from the same publication and are not independent witnesses. The list gives no dates or spouses for the children and does not establish an interleaved birth order. Each percentage concerns the specific father-profile pair, with later adult identity assessed separately. William’s own father remains unknown and unrated; Adam-3151 remains 77% probable because the 1834/1840 birth claims and Arthur’s Ohio-born son Adam-2387 are unresolved. Henry Cunningham-3148 and Isaac Watts-3149 remain 92%. No maternal assessment, structured vital field, selected father ID or live WikiTree flag is changed.

historical_basis.reason: The historical paragraph lists the eight children before their mother’s explicitly dated20March1890death. This is a conservative privacy bound, not a new individual birth estimate; retained profile birth dates are1824–1844.

note: The original 1851 Glenleslie household 21 return records John Glasgow as 100, Rose as 80, and 1791 for both. Its marriage heading asks “In what Year Married, or in what Years if more than once?” The detailed transcription’s first-marriage field is therefore an editorial description, not the literal question on this return. Only 1791 is entered: an earlier union is not documented, and the request for multiple years means its absence still weighs against a straightforward earlier-marriage explanation. The original also calls the forty-year-old John a nephew and gives his occupation as vagrant; the 1839 marriage belongs to him. The mortality table explicitly calls Andrew Glasgow, a thirty-year-old linen weaver who died of consumption in winter 1848, a son of the head. It does not name Andrew’s mother. 38% assesses the complete John-to-Robert profile hypothesis, not the certainty of reading the census. Robert’s census-implied birth about 1778–1779 precedes the sole reported marriage year by roughly twelve years. An earlier union, nonmarital fatherhood or a reporting error would still be needed, and none is established. The original asks for multiple marriage years, so omission of an earlier year remains a real limitation. John’s exceptional age may be inaccurate. An uncle, cousin, other collateral relative or unrepresented father remains possible; the older Alexander comparison is not excluded. Rose’s reported age does not fit her as Robert’s mother, and no mother or earlier wife is assigned. The selection concerns the 1851 Glenleslie man only: it does not identify him with the Lisnagaver tithe occupier, validate every attached child, or prove a Y-DNA pedigree. Hugh-3956’s 74% brother hypothesis includes a separate identity uncertainty and is not automatically assigned this father; his estimated earlier generation also needs its own chronology test. The inherited Unknown Glasgow-3905 is preserved as an uncertain alternative with no invented percentage. No live WikiTree family field is changed.

assessment:
**Original will, 23 October 2026:** Samuel Glasgow of West Fallowfield names wife **Tabitha**, infant daughter **Margaret Ellen**, and a contingent remainder to the **sons of his three brothers William, James and Robert Glasgow, of Ireland**. The three named men are the testator’s brothers; the beneficiaries are their sons. This is not a clause naming the testator’s own son James. The will is dated **17 May 1824**; the proving endorsement is **31 May 1824**. [County original](https://portal.laserfiche.com/Portal/DocView.aspx?id=773006&page=588&repo=r-24f48cc6), file 7520, scanned volume 07451–7600, portal pp. 588–589 (downloaded extract pp. 3–4). Cover is portal p. 586. Original pages were visually read; the brother clause was independently reread.

The will appoints Robert Futhey and Thomas Stewart executors; estate office does not establish kinship. It also names Samuel Glasgow Haslett, described as James Haslett’s infant twin son; no godparent relationship is stated. His Glasgow middle name does not make him a Glasgow son. Later accounts, portal pp. 594 and 596, name Benjamin Glasgow as a debtor and William Glasgow in transmitting another estate’s legacy, without stating their relationship to the testator.

**Profile identity:** [Samuel Glasgow-2872](/people/glasgow-2872.html) remains a compatible candidate, not an established identification. His retained Cochranville locality and exact 17 May 1824 date fit this estate closely, but that date is the will date and may have been inherited as a death date. The will alone cannot prove death on that day. The profile’s Judith, who died in 1812, does not exclude a later Tabitha marriage. Its Pennsylvania birth/parent reconstruction and the brothers in Ireland need a combined family test rather than an automatic rejection or merge. No other local Tabitha or Margaret Ellen catalogue identity was found in the bounded duplicate check. The existing 72% father assessment and all family/vital fields are retained; this source does not name the testator’s father.

**Missouri comparison:** [James Glasgow-45](/people/glasgow-45.html), the probable Downington-born drummer, is not named in the inspected will or later accounts. That absence does not establish that he was not a son, but neither the military entry nor this estate selects a named father. The new Ireland relatives supply a concrete family to investigate while the immigrant-father/Philadelphia-estate tradition remains unproved. The complete downloaded estate extract is retained privately; no manuscript image is republished.

assessment:
**Original-page review, 23 October 2026:** [Gibson’s printed p. 414](https://ia903202.us.archive.org/BookReader/BookReaderImages.php?zip=/18/items/historyofyorkcou00gibs/historyofyorkcou00gibs_jp2.zip&file=historyofyorkcou00gibs_jp2/historyofyorkcou00gibs_0512.jp2&id=historyofyorkcou00gibs&scale=1&rotate=0) gives Hugh’s exact 8 September 1769 Nottingham birth and says his unnamed father emigrated about 1730 and died at Nottingham in 1772. Hugh was the third son and the only one to reach adulthood. The page does **not** name John, Mary Cranmer, Sarah or the earlier sons; its storekeeper account concerns Hugh. Those names must not be attributed to this page. It is an original scan of a late 1886 compilation, not an original eighteenth-century birth or death entry. Its informant and independence from later family tradition are unknown.

The retained John-2871 remains the leading named father hypothesis for Hugh. The reviewed Chester tax index lists John with 80 acres in West Nottingham in 1787–1791 and Hugh with 80 acres in 1793–1799, after John’s recorded 1792 death. That consecutive name, locality and acreage pattern supports family succession, but the tax index is not a conveyance proving the same parcel or a father–son relationship. The newly inspected Gibson p. 414 names neither parent and instead says Hugh’s father emigrated about 1730 and died in 1772. Those dates conflict with John-2871’s retained 1738 birth and 1792 death. The late history may contain errors, so the existing father remains probable, but its general Nottingham context cannot be counted as independent agreement on this particular John. File 4225 independently documents a John’s 1792 East Nottingham estate; it does not name Hugh in the inspected surviving papers.

82% is an individual subjective estimate for Hugh-2873 → John-2871, reduced from 94% after original-page review. The index succession remains useful circumstantial evidence; the unnamed 1886 paternal account is substantive counterevidence. Neither John-2870 nor the 1789 shoemaker is selected as a replacement. No parent is detached, and no vital field or mother is changed.

The 1730/1772 account does not identify John-2870 either: child migration in 1730 would fit his 1722 baptism, but the retained May 1769 death conflicts with 1772. A September 1769 Hugh birth after a May death would permit posthumous fatherhood and is not an exclusion. No replacement father or mother follows.

Gibson’s inspected printed p. 414 explicitly calls Cunningham R. Glasgow the congressman Hugh Glasgow’s son and locates his farm about a mile south of the old Glasgow homestead, on the Maryland side of the Mason–Dixon line. The existing Cunningham Ramsay-3742, born 1806, is the adult son of that distinctive name in Hugh’s family. The other Cunningham, Sample-3747, died in infancy and cannot be the mature farmer described. The specific name, recorded father, adult generation and family locality identify the existing pair strongly beyond the earlier memorial/profile reconstruction.

97% is a confident identification of the existing father–child profile pair from an explicit son statement in a late compiled history. It is not a newly discovered birth entry. The book’s present-tense description may reflect information gathered before its 1886 publication; the profile’s retained 1885 death is not corrected to 1886. No mother, exact vital date, parent attachment or live WikiTree flag is changed.

assessment:
**Two original estates, not one John:** [file 4015](https://portal.laserfiche.com/Portal/DocView.aspx?id=772934&page=1065&repo=r-24f48cc6), West Nottingham, contains an administration bond dated 31 March 1789, an inventory dated 26 March, and Peter Glasgow’s signed certificate of 26 March. Peter says the deceased John lived at his house about 27 years, was his uncle, and died intestate. Peter asks that John Taylor, **Peter’s sister’s son**, administer. The bond appoints John Taylor; William Edmonston and Henry McCormick are securities, not kin established by their office. The inventory includes eleven old shoemaker lasts. The next estate begins at portal p. 1067. [Complete connected family drafts and candidate review](/research/subjects/nottingham-probate/#john-shoemaker).

[File 4225](https://portal.laserfiche.com/Portal/DocView.aspx?id=772936&page=247&repo=r-24f48cc6), East Nottingham, has an inventory dated **31 May 1792**, followed by its June oath. Portal p. 249 includes a debt against the estate of **John Glasgow, shoemaker, deceased**. The distinctive occupation, earlier death and nearby place make the 1789 uncle a probable identification of this deceased debtor; the debt does not prove the two Johns were related. The file’s replacement slip says the original administration bond is missing and directs the reader to **Administration Book 2, p. 386**. The next estate begins at portal p. 251. The surviving file does not supply a named Hugh heir.

John-2871, whose death is recorded in 1792, is a compatible candidate for the 1792 estate, with an East/West Nottingham locality question still open. The 1789 uncle cannot be assigned to John-2870 (retained death 1769) or John-2871 (1792) without resolving those actual conflicts. No generic name match, estate office or debt is converted into a father relationship. The inventory and bond dates are not exact death dates.

note: The original 1860 census, Richland Township, Belmont County, Ohio, page 90, dwelling 626/family 634, lines 26–28, records John Glassga, male, 86, born Ireland, personal estate $150; Elizabeth, 61, born Maryland; and Daniel E, 24, farmer, born Ohio. The distinctive Daniel E, age, place and Elizabeth identify the maintained Ohio family. The schedule has no relationship column: it does not itself state that Daniel is John’s son or name John’s parents. The East Richland Cemetery photograph shows John Glasgow, died Jan. 8, 1864, in his 92nd year. This implies about 1772–1773, whereas the census age implies about 1773–1774. The weathered inscription and reported ages do not establish an exact birthday. Find a Grave’s typed fields instead give 26 November 1784 and Bathgate; its own narrative says 92, exposing an internal conflict. Findmypast’s Wiston and Roberton transcript, OPR 660/1, item 1, gives John Glasgow born 26 November 1784, baptised 30 November, father James Glasgow, residence transcribed “?Shield”; no mother is supplied. Its exact birthday matches the modern Ohio fields, but that precision is not independent identity evidence: the original Ohio census and monument indicate a man roughly a decade older, and the census says Ireland. The source of the typed birthday and Bathgate place has not been established. Prefer the Irish adult evidence and do not attach James or Peter Glasgow. The Wiston child’s later identity remains unresolved; this review does not assign that record to the Canongate man Glasgow-1460 either.

One memorial version gives Janet16October1853 aged76, consistent with that birth generation; the other gives1873 aged76, implying1797, after the explicitly named mother’s1795 death. Prefer the1853/76 interpretation as coherent with the recorded family while retaining1873 as a competing reading. The existing Janet-1448 account is defined only by this Thomas/Christian family and the same memorial citation, with no independently documented conflicting adult household. Its inherited Bridgeton, Kincardineshire birthplace and Blackburn surname are unverified, not evidence of a distinct daughter. Assess the existing father at97% from43% and the existing named mother at97% as her first individual rating. The preferred death year and parent confidence are one combined argument, not independent corroborations. Existing birth boundary and places are retained. No parent attachment, identity merge, or change to Thomas-1023’s own ancestry follows. Original stone and parish register uninspected; all memorial index rows concern one monument and are not independent witnesses. A misread year or age remains possible, including1873 with a different age. Blackburn follows Janet’s name and may denote residence; no husband, married surname or new natal place is established. Preserve the current birth boundary, birthplace and surname pending separate evidence. The preferred death reading and parent identification share the same combined evidence; neither is newly discovered independent proof of the other. No new parent attachment or identity merge is made. On 1 July 1817 Alexander Glasgow, merchant in Wilson’s Court, Argyle Street, entered as eldest son of John Glasgow, merchant and burgess/guild brother (p.306, PDF 316). On 3 May 1844 John Glasgow, merchant, entered as a younger son of John Glasgow, merchant and burgess/guild brother (p.450, PDF 460). The first entry strongly identifies the maintained John-1348/Helen Smith household; the sons are supported comparisons with Alexander-971 and John-1355. The sons’ entries do not name their mother, and the three admissions must not be treated as a literal statement that all three men form one family. These are inspected published register transcriptions; the underlying manuscript admission registers are unread. Burke’s Visitation, vol.2, printed armorial section p.67 (PDF 341), has now been read in the scan. It explicitly describes Alexander of Old Court, formerly Auchinraith, as eldest son of the late John Glasgow and Helen, daughter of James Smith, and grandson of Alexander Glasgow, merchant, and Agnes Monro of Edinburgh. The family passage was already quoted in the held biography; inspecting it is not discovery of a previously unknown grandfather name. The underlying Lyon matriculation remains unread. Burke names Agnes Monro, not the documented Mary Munro of Alexander-1309’s couple. Their identity cannot be assumed, and the 1771 child has no inspected occupation, wife or estate bridge identifying him as the merchant rather than the Colinton account John-1304. The merchant’s circa 1770 birth is an inherited estimate, not independent corroboration. Retain both modern Johns and the current father selection, all mothers, vital fields and upstream grades. No new father attachment or merge follows. The 1741 childhood identification of Alexander-1309 is not certified by this review.
